name: Machu Picchu
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The Inca royal estate on a green saddle between two Andean peaks above a hairpin loop of the Urubamba River, Peru. T1: it sits at ~2,430 m (7,970 ft), so often wreathed in cloud it's called the 'cloud city'; the sharp peak looming behind the classic postcard view is Huayna Picchu (answer = the named peak; distractors Salkantay, Ausangate, Huascaran). T2 (honest-stance payoff): when Yale's Hiram Bingham was led up in 1911 by a local farmer, the ruins were NOT empty -- Quechua families (Richarte, Alvarez) were already farming the terraces, and Agustin Lizarraga had carved his name there in 1902 (answer = local people already lived/farmed there; it was never a 'lost' place to them). T3: unlike Cusco, Machu Picchu escaped one fate that hit almost every Inca site -- the Spanish conquistadors never found it (answer = never reached/looted by Spain). T4: carved from the living bedrock at the summit is a single granite pillar whose shadow marks the solstice, the 'hitching post of the sun' -- the Intihuatana (answer = named ritual stone; teach the term; distractors the Torreon, a chacana, a huaca). T5 (dinner-test payoff): about 60% of the building effort here is invisible -- deep buried foundations and a hidden crushed-rock drainage system that keeps the terraced city from sliding off a wet, fault-riddled ridge (answer = the underground engineering). Further rungs: the curved Temple of the Sun (Torreon) whose window catches the June-solstice sunrise on a sacred rock; mortarless ashlar walls with inward-leaning trapezoidal doorways that shrug off earthquakes; built ~1450 as emperor Pachacuti's country estate, not a legendary lost city; the agricultural terraces (andenes) that both fed it and stabilised the slope; its place on the Qhapaq Nan Inca road; the fault-line siting that gave the Inca pre-fractured stone to quarry.
source: Wikipedia: Machu Picchu (elev 2,430 m; built ~1450 under Pachacuti, occupied ~1420-1530; Spanish never found it; Bingham 1911 led by Melchor Arteaga, found Richarte & Alvarez families farming; Lizarraga 1902; Intihuatana solstice stone; Temple of the Sun/Torreon; dry ashlar masonry) -- verified via WebFetch. Underground-drainage 'invisible 60%' from Kenneth Wright's engineering studies. Build-stage cross-check on Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) recommended as primary.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER, celebrate Inca engineering as real achievement (never 'mysterious lost race'). Lead with the cloud-wreathed setting, never 'What is Machu Picchu?'. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: Bingham did not 'discover' it -- locals lived there and Lizarraga preceded him in 1902; frame the 1911 rung honestly so it doesn't erase the people already there. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 hidden drainage (most of the work is underground). LANE: Inca-empire politics and the Spanish conquest belong to HISTORY -- keep every rung anchored to the PLACE and its engineering (drainage, Intihuatana, terraces, never-found-by-Spain), not a Pachacuti biography or conquest narrative.
history_overlap: Pachacuti's reign and the Spanish conquest of the Inca are history-bank episodes. Keep rungs on the site's engineering/setting; the T2 'Bingham 1911' rung must anchor on the PLACE (locals already there / never found by Spain), not a conquest or biography ladder.

name: Teotihuacan
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The vast ruined metropolis 40 km northeast of modern Mexico City, in the Valley of Mexico. T1: a dead-straight ceremonial avenue over 2 km long runs through the heart of the city, lined with platforms the much-later Aztecs mistook for royal tombs -- so they named it the Avenue of the Dead (answer = the named avenue; distractors other Mesoamerican causeways/sacbeob). T2 (the striking unknown): around 500 CE this was one of the largest cities on Earth, home to 100,000+ people, yet one basic thing is lost forever -- what its own builders called themselves and their city (answer = the builders' name/identity is unknown; 'Teotihuacan' is the Nahuatl name the Aztecs gave the ruins centuries later, meaning roughly 'place where the gods were made'). T3: rising about 65 m over the avenue, the third-largest ancient pyramid in all the Americas is the Pyramid of the Sun (answer = the named pyramid; distractors Pyramid of the Moon, the Great Pyramid of Cholula, La Danta at El Mirador). T4 (dinner-test payoff): in 2015 archaeologist Sergio Gomez tunnelled beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent and found, sealed for ~1,800 years, pools of a shimmering liquid metal -- liquid mercury, plus jade, mica and carved shells, perhaps an underworld river (answer = the liquid mercury). T5: the whole city is deliberately tilted ~15.5 degrees east of north on a single grid, and the Pyramid of the Moon squares up to face the sacred mountain Cerro Gordo behind it (answer = the astronomical/mountain alignment of the city plan). Further rungs: the Temple of the Feathered Serpent's facade bristling with stone Quetzalcoatl heads; multi-family stone apartment compounds housing artisans; workshops of green Pachuca obsidian traded across Mesoamerica; brilliant murals like the 'Paradise of Tlaloc'; the city's mysterious burning and collapse ~550 CE.
source: Wikipedia: Pyramid of the Sun (~65.5 m, third-largest ancient pyramid in the New World after La Danta & Cholula; Aztecs named it, the Teotihuacanos' own name unknown; Avenue of the Dead) -- verified via WebFetch. Liquid-mercury tunnel discovery = Sergio Gomez, INAH, 2015 (Temple of the Feathered Serpent). Peak population 100,000+ and ~15.5-degree grid tilt from the Teotihuacan main article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; present a real, sophisticated human city -- the 'we don't even know their name' rung is genuine wonder, NOT 'aliens/lost race' exoticising (that's the failure mode the stance rebuts). Lead with the Avenue scene. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: 'Teotihuacan' and 'Pyramid of the Sun' are LATER Aztec/Nahuatl names -- the builders' own names are unknown; the mercury is a real 2015 find, not legend. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the liquid-mercury tunnel (T4). LANE: the Aztecs are a HISTORY people -- keep rungs on the PLACE (avenue, pyramids, mercury, city grid); the unknown-builders rung is a place-mystery, not Aztec history.
history_overlap: Aztec history is history-bank; here the Aztecs appear only as the later namers of the ruins. Keep every rung on the site itself. Flag the 'unknown builders' rung so it reads as a place-mystery rather than duplicating an Aztec-history ladder.

name: Tenochtitlan
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The Aztec (Mexica) island capital in Lake Texcoco, now buried beneath Mexico City. T1: in 1325 the Mexica founded their capital where they saw a prophesied omen -- an eagle on a cactus (the image now on Mexico's flag) -- on an island in Lake Texcoco (answer = the named lake; distractors Lake Titicaca, Lake Patzcuaro, Lake Chapala). T2: to feed a city with no farmland, the Mexica staked rectangular beds of mud and reeds into the shallow lakebed, so fertile they cropped year-round -- floating gardens called chinampas (answer = the named farming feature; teach the term; distractors Inca andenes, waru waru, milpa). T3: three broad raised roads tied the island to the shore and a twin terracotta aqueduct piped fresh spring water in from Chapultepec (answer = the causeways-and-aqueduct water system / the named spring). T4: Cortes's soldiers in 1519 said the city -- larger than any in Spain, home to 200,000+ -- looked like an enchantment; at its centre stood a great twin-shrined pyramid to the war god and the rain god, the Templo Mayor (answer = the named great temple; distractors the Caracol, the Pyramid of the Sun, El Castillo). T5 (dinner-test payoff): Mexico City today sinks by as much as tens of centimetres a year and its cathedral visibly tilts -- because after razing Tenochtitlan in 1521 the Spanish drained Lake Texcoco, and the modern city sits on the soft, compacting old lakebed (answer = the drained lake / subsidence). Further rungs: Moctezuma's zoo, aviary and botanical gardens; the sister-market of Tlatelolco drawing tens of thousands of traders a day; the sacred precinct; the Templo Mayor rediscovered in 1978 by electrical workers digging downtown.
source: Wikipedia: Tenochtitlan (founded 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco; eagle-and-cactus founding legend now on the flag; chinampas; three causeways to Tepeyac/Iztapalapa/Tlacopan; twin aqueduct from Chapultepec springs; peak population 200,000-400,000; Templo Mayor to Huitzilopochtli & Tlaloc; Cortes 8 Nov 1519, razed 1521; drained lakebed causes modern subsidence) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate the island city's engineering (a metropolis larger than contemporary European capitals) without triumphalism, and be honest BOTH ways about 1521 (a real razing AND a real epidemic collapse), never a theatrical morality tale. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the eagle-on-cactus is the FOUNDING LEGEND (say so); population figures are estimates. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 drained-lake subsidence (why Mexico City sinks). LANE: Cortes and the conquest are HISTORY -- keep rungs on the PLACE (island setting, chinampas, causeways, Templo Mayor, the sinking city); the 1521 rung must land on the LAKE/subsidence wonder, not retell the conquest.
history_overlap: The Spanish conquest is a history-bank episode. Keep rungs on the city's geography and engineering; the razing rung must anchor on the drained-lake subsidence payoff, not a conquest narrative that duplicates a history ladder.

name: Chichen Itza
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The great Maya city of the Yucatan, Mexico, famed for its serpent-shadow pyramid. T1: the step-pyramid at the city's centre, El Castillo, has 91 steps on each of its four sides -- add the top platform and the count reaches exactly 365, one per day of the year (answer = 365, the calendar-in-stone; number built as payoff; distractors 360, 260 the Maya ritual count, 584 the Venus cycle -- all real Maya numbers). T2 (dinner-test payoff): twice a year, on the spring and autumn equinox, the late-afternoon sun throws a zigzag of triangular shadows down El Castillo's north staircase so a giant snake seems to slither to the carved stone serpent-head at the base -- the descent of Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent (answer = Kukulkan / the equinox serpent shadow; distractors Chaac, Itzamna, Quetzalcoatl). T3: Chichen Itza holds the largest ball court in the ancient Americas -- about 168 m long, stone scoring-rings set high on the walls, acoustics that carry a whisper end to end -- the Great Ball Court (answer = the named court / its record size). T4: into a huge natural limestone sinkhole at the city's edge the Maya cast gold, jade and human offerings to the rain god Chaac; divers still dredge treasure and bone from this Sacred Cenote -- a cenote being a collapsed-limestone sinkhole exposing groundwater in a land with no rivers (answer = a cenote / the Sacred Cenote; teach the karst term). T5: clap once at the foot of El Castillo and the staircase answers with a strange chirp that researchers say mimics the sacred quetzal bird -- an echo created as the evenly spaced steps diffract the sound (answer = the chirped-echo acoustic effect). Further rungs: an older pyramid with a red jaguar throne nested inside El Castillo; the round Caracol tower aligned to the motions of Venus; the Temple of the Warriors with its reclining Chac Mool.
source: Wikipedia: El Castillo, Chichen Itza (91 steps x4 + top platform = 365; equinox late-afternoon triangular shadows create the illusion of the feathered serpent crawling down; 24 m + 6 m temple = 30 m; nested inner pyramid ~600-800 CE) -- verified via WebFetch. Great Ball Court (largest in Mesoamerica, ~168 m), Sacred Cenote, and the staircase quetzal-chirp echo (David Lubman's acoustic studies) from the Chichen Itza article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Maya astronomy as sophisticated real science (the 365-step calendar, the equinox alignment) -- no 'ancient aliens'. Lead with the scene, never 'How many steps...'. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the serpent-shadow and the quetzal-chirp echo are REAL, observable effects, not legend; count the 365 steps 'including the top platform' (some steps are eroded). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T2 equinox serpent shadow. LANE: Maya astronomy/history is shared -- keep rungs on the built PLACE (El Castillo, the shadow, the ball court, the cenote, the acoustics); the cenote also cross-links to Yucatan karst geology, which is geography's own.
history_overlap: Maya astronomy and dynastic history overlap with the history bank. Keep rungs on the site's built marvels and the equinox effect; frame the Sacred-Cenote sacrifices respectfully and factually, not as a history episode.

name: Tikal
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A Maya superpower city lost for a thousand years in the Peten rainforest of northern Guatemala. T1: six steep temple-pyramids punch up through the jungle at Tikal; the tallest, Temple IV, lifts its roof-comb about 70 m -- high enough to rise clear ABOVE the rainforest canopy, so climbers look out over an unbroken green sea of treetops (answer = above the forest canopy; distractors below the water table, into a cliff, over a gorge). T2: across the Great Plaza two twin pyramids face off -- the funerary Temple I, the 'Temple of the Great Jaguar' built over a king's tomb, gazes at Temple II, the 'Temple of the Masks' (answer = the named twin temple). T3: this was a lost city that truly vanished -- after ~900 CE the Maya abandoned Tikal and the jungle swallowed it for a millennium; the leading (still-debated) trigger across the Maya lowlands was decades of severe drought worsened by deforestation (answer = the drought-driven collapse; flag as leading-but-debated). T4: carved monuments record Tikal's centuries-long war with a rival superpower to the north, the 'Snake Kingdom' -- the dynasty of Calakmul (answer = the named rival city; distractors Copan, Palenque, Caracol). T5 (dinner-test payoff): with no rivers or lakes, Tikal's builders paved vast plazas to funnel every rainfall into lined reservoirs, and study of the largest suggests they kept the water clean with quartz sand and filtering plants -- an early water-filtration system (answer = the reservoir/sand-filter engineering). Further rungs: the towering plaster roof-combs; layered royal tombs in the North Acropolis; king Jasaw Chan K'awiil I's defeat of Calakmul in 695; Temple IV commissioned by Yikin Chan K'awiil ~741.
source: Wikipedia: Tikal Temple IV (70 m to top of roof-comb; the SECOND-tallest pre-Columbian structure still standing, after Tonina's pyramid, with Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun possibly once taller; built ~741 for Yikin Chan K'awiil) -- verified via WebFetch, correcting the common 'tallest' claim. Tikal reservoir sand-filtration = 2020 PNAS/Univ. of Cincinnati study. Calakmul rivalry and drought-collapse from the Tikal article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Maya engineering and astronomy as a full civilization. KEY ACCURACY RAIL (research-caught): do NOT call Temple IV 'the tallest pre-Columbian structure' -- it is roughly second (Tonina/Cholula/Pyramid of the Sun contest it); say 'one of the tallest, rising above the canopy'. Frame the collapse as the leading-but-debated drought explanation. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 rainwater reservoirs with sand filtration. LANE: the Tikal-Calakmul dynastic wars are a HISTORY subject -- frame the T4 rival rung as a PLACE (the rival city) not a war narrative, to avoid duplicating a history ladder.
history_overlap: Tikal-Calakmul dynastic warfare risks duplicating a history ladder. Frame the Calakmul rung as a place (the rival city on the horizon) and keep the rest on the canopy-piercing temples, reservoirs, and the rainforest reclaiming the city.

name: Cahokia
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A vast earthen mound-city on the Mississippi floodplain across from modern St. Louis, Illinois -- the largest city north of Mexico in its day. T1: a thousand years ago the biggest city in what is now the United States rose here, built not of stone but of earth -- more than 100 flat-topped platform mounds raised one woven basket of soil at a time (answer = the earthen mounds; teach 'platform mound'; distractors stone pyramids, ziggurats, kivas). T2: its centrepiece, Monks Mound, climbs about 30 m (100 ft) in four broad terraces and spreads across a base as large as the Great Pyramid of Giza -- roughly 13 acres (answer = the Great Pyramid of Giza comparison; number built as payoff; distractors a city block, a football field, the Colosseum). T3: at its ~1100 CE peak Cahokia may have held 10,000-20,000 people, making it larger at that moment than the London of the time (answer = London; flag population as an estimate; distractors Paris, Rome, Constantinople). T4: west of Monks Mound, postholes trace great rings of upright red-cedar posts that framed the sunrise across the seasons -- a wooden solar calendar nicknamed Woodhenge (answer = the named calendar circle; distractors Stonehenge, the Sun Dagger, a medicine wheel). T5 (dinner-test payoff): in Mound 72 a leader was laid out on a bed of some 20,000 shell beads arranged in the shape of a falcon-man, ringed by rows of sacrificed attendants -- the 'Birdman' burial, proof of a powerful ranked society (answer = the falcon/Birdman bead burial). Further rungs: a two-mile log palisade wall; trade goods of marine shell and Great Lakes copper reaching Cahokia; abandonment by ~1350 (flood/climate/resource stress, debated); the name 'Cahokia' is a later borrowing -- the builders' own name is unknown.
source: Wikipedia: Monks Mound (~30 m high; base 291 m x 236 m; base footprint 'roughly the same size' as the Great Pyramid of Giza ~13.1 acres; four terraces; largest pre-Columbian earthwork in the Americas and largest pyramid north of Mesoamerica) -- verified via WebFetch. Peak population 10,000-20,000 and 'larger than contemporary London', Woodhenge, and the Mound 72 Birdman burial (~20,000 shell beads) from the Cahokia article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; explicitly a FULL civilization -- the 'bigger than London' fact rebuts the 'primitive mound-builders' myth (config names Cahokia as celebrated). KEY ACCURACY RAIL (research-caught): Monks Mound's base RIVALS Giza's footprint -- it is NOT taller or larger overall; and the population is an ESTIMATE ('may have held', 'larger than the London of the time'). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 Birdman burial on 20,000 shell beads. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (mounds, Woodhenge, Mound 72); Mississippian culture broadly is shared with history.
history_overlap: Mississippian culture overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the earthworks themselves; flag the 'bigger than London' rung as an estimate and anchor it to Monks Mound, not a general Mississippian-history ladder.

name: Easter Island (Rapa Nui)
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A tiny volcanic island in the far southeastern Pacific -- the most remote inhabited island on Earth. T1: on an island ~3,500 km from the nearest mainland, the Rapanui carved about 900 giant stone figures with heavy brows and long torsos, most gazing inland over their villages -- the moai (answer = the named statues; teach the term; distractors tiki, ahu, pukao). T2: almost every moai was cut from the soft volcanic tuff of a single crater, where hundreds still stand half-finished in the slopes -- the quarry of Rano Raraku (answer = the named quarry; distractors Rano Kau, Puna Pau, Terevaka). T3: the moai stand on stone platforms called ahu; the most famous line is the fifteen restored giants standing shoulder to shoulder at Ahu Tongariki (answer = the named platform row; distractors Anakena, Orongo, Vinapu). T4 (dinner-test payoff): Rapanui oral tradition says the moai 'walked' from the quarry to their platforms upright, and in 2012 archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested it -- a small crew rocked an upright replica side to side with three ropes so it waddled forward on its own base (answer = 'walked' upright by rope-rocking; LABEL as oral tradition + experiment; distractors rolled on logs, dragged on sledges, floated -- all real proposed methods). T5: some moai once wore a red stone topknot (pukao) quarried from a different red-scoria pit, Puna Pau; later, in a time of upheaval, the Rapanui toppled the moai and turned to a new faith -- the Birdman (Tangata manu) cult, whose egg-gathering contest was held on the sea-cliffs at Orongo (answer = the Birdman cult; distractors a sun cult, an ancestor cult, a whale cult). Further rungs: the moai's inlaid eyes of white coral with obsidian or red-scoria pupils; the undeciphered rongorongo script; the crater lake of Rano Kau; and the CONTESTED 'collapse' story -- Jared Diamond's deforestation-'ecocide' versus Hunt & Lipo's case that Polynesian rats plus later slave-raids and disease did most of the damage.
source: Wikipedia: Moai (>900 statues; carved from Rano Raraku tuff; tallest erected 'Paro' ~10 m / 82 tonnes; largest unfinished ~21 m; pukao red scoria from Puna Pau; coral-and-obsidian/scoria eyes) -- verified via WebFetch. 'Walking' moai: oral tradition plus the 2012 Terry Hunt & Carl Lipo rope-rocking experiment (and the 1986 Pavel/Heyerdahl precedent). Ahu Tongariki (15 moai), the Orongo Birdman cult, and the Diamond-vs-Hunt/Lipo collapse debate from the Easter Island / Rapa Nui articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the moai are a cultural creation born on this island -- geography owns the island, the quarries, and the moving of the stones. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the moai 'walked' per ORAL TRADITION and a rope-rocking EXPERIMENT -- say both, never state it as plain fact; and label the 'ecocide' collapse story as CONTESTED (don't cast the Rapanui as fools who doomed themselves -- that is exactly the condescension the stance rebuts). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T4 walking moai. LANE: no animal or food rung -- this is the island and its statues.
history_overlap: The 'collapse' debate touches anthropology/history. Keep rungs on the island and its statues (quarry, ahu, walking, pukao, Birdman); flag the ecocide rung as genuinely contested and frame the walking as oral-tradition-plus-experiment.

name: Cusco and Sacsayhuaman
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The Inca capital Cusco (Qosqo) high in the Peruvian Andes and its great hilltop stronghold, Sacsayhuaman. T1 (dinner-test payoff): the Inca called their capital Qosqo, 'the navel of the world', and laid the whole city out in the shape of a crouching puma, with the huge zigzag ramparts of Sacsayhuaman forming its head (answer = the puma-shaped city; distractors a condor, a serpent, a jaguar). T2: Sacsayhuaman's walls are built from limestone blocks so vast the largest is estimated at 100-200 tonnes, yet fitted so precisely, without mortar, that not even a knife blade or sheet of paper slips into the joints (answer = the paper-thin mortarless joints; distractors 'they used no metal tools', 'the walls lean inward', 'each block is unique'). T3: in a Cusco street stands a single Inca block cut to interlock with its neighbours on twelve separate sides -- the famous 'twelve-angled stone' (answer = twelve; number as payoff; distractors 6, 8, 14). T4: when a great earthquake levelled much of colonial Cusco in 1950, the Spanish buildings crumbled while the Inca walls beneath them stood unharmed -- Inca masonry, with trapezoidal doorways and inward-leaning interlocked blocks, is built to ride out quakes (answer = the Inca walls survived where the Spanish ones fell). T5: the Spanish tore down the Inca Sun Temple, the Qorikancha -- whose walls had been sheathed in sheets of gold and which held a golden garden -- and raised the church of Santo Domingo directly on its flawless Inca foundations (answer = the gold-sheathed Sun Temple). Further rungs: Cusco as the hub of the Qhapaq Nan, the 40,000 km Inca road network; the theory that Sacsayhuaman's zigzag walls form the puma's teeth; blocks shaped by pounding with harder hammerstones, not sawing; the 1536 siege of Sacsayhuaman.
source: Wikipedia: Sacsayhuaman (three terrace walls ~6 m tall, longest ~400 m; largest limestone block estimated 128 to ~200 tonnes; 'a single piece of paper will not fit between many of the stones', Cieza de Leon on the joints; Cusco imagined as a puma with Sacsayhuaman as the head; ~3,701 m; built under Pachacuti) -- verified via WebFetch. Twelve-angled stone (Hatunrumiyoc), the 1950 earthquake, and the gold-sheathed Qorikancha/Santo Domingo from the Cusco & Qorikancha articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the perfect-fit stonework is celebrated Inca engineering -- the failure mode is 'aliens/too advanced for the Inca' pseudo-archaeology, which the stance directly rebuts (config names Sacsayhuaman). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: block weights are ESTIMATES; the Inca shaped stone with stone hammers, ramps and human labour -- not aliens. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 puma-city / T2 paper-thin joints. LANE: the Inca empire and the conquest are HISTORY -- keep rungs on the PLACES (puma plan, Sacsayhuaman's stones, the twelve-angled stone, earthquake-proof walls, gold-sheathed Qorikancha); frame the 1536 siege as the place, not a battle narrative.
history_overlap: The Inca empire, Pachacuti, and the Spanish conquest are history-bank. Keep rungs on the stonework and city plan; frame the 1536 siege rung as the fortress-place, preferring the engineering angle so it doesn't duplicate a conquest ladder.

name: Palenque
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A jewel-like Maya city on a jungle escarpment in Chiapas, Mexico, hiding one of the great tombs of the ancient world. T1: Palenque's grandest pyramid conceals a secret under its floor -- a rubble-choked stairway plunging deep into the structure; it is named for the long carved text on its summit temple, the Temple of the Inscriptions (answer = the named temple; distractors Temple of the Cross, of the Sun, of the Foliated Cross). T2: over 1948-1952 archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier cleared that buried stair and broke through to something no one thought Maya pyramids held -- a sealed royal tomb deep inside, overturning the idea that these pyramids were only temples (answer = an intact tomb inside the pyramid). T3 (dinner-test payoff): the king's coffin is sealed by a 5-tonne carved limestone lid showing him at the instant of death, falling into the underworld along the branches of the Maya World Tree -- popularly and wrongly nicknamed 'the astronaut' (answer = the World Tree / the ceiba, NOT an astronaut; distractors a jaguar throne, a feathered serpent, a maize god). T4: the king in that tomb, Pakal, ruled Palenque for an astonishing ~68 years (615-683 CE), long enough to rebuild it into a masterpiece of light, airy Maya architecture (answer = ~68 years, one of the longest reigns of the ancient world; number as payoff; distractors ~20, ~40, ~90). T5: Palenque's palace has a feature found at no other Maya city -- a four-storey square tower rising over the plaza, perhaps for watching the sky (answer = the palace tower; distractors a ball court, a pyramid, a causeway). Further rung: the Maya vaulted the Otulum stream into a stone aqueduct beneath the palace, creating the earliest known water pressure in the Americas.
source: Wikipedia: Temple of the Inscriptions (Ruz removed the floor slab in 1952 to reveal the rubble-filled stairway, cleared over two years, to Pakal's tomb; the sarcophagus lid shows Pakal between the heavens/Cosmic Tree and the underworld; Pakal's reign 'almost 70 years'; 617-glyph inscription, one of the longest Maya texts) -- verified via WebFetch. Palace four-storey tower and Otulum aqueduct from the Palenque article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the sarcophagus lid is Pakal at the Maya World Tree -- the T3 rung must EXPLICITLY correct the 'ancient astronaut' misreading (the flagship pseudo-archaeology case), crediting Maya cosmology. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: Ruz reached the tomb in 1952 (stair cleared 1948-52); the lid is the World Tree, not a spaceman. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 lid / 'astronaut' correction. LANE: Pakal's reign is a HISTORY/biography topic -- anchor the T2/T4 rungs on the TOMB-inside-a-pyramid discovery and the site, not a Pakal life-story ladder.
history_overlap: Pakal's reign is a history-bank biography. Keep rungs on the site (the hidden tomb, the lid, the palace tower, the aqueduct); the Pakal rungs must anchor on the tomb discovery, not duplicate a Pakal biography ladder.

name: Nazca Lines
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: Enormous drawings scraped across the bone-dry Nazca Desert on Peru's southern coast. T1: on one of the driest plateaus on Earth, ancient people drew pictures so vast that most can only be seen whole from the air, hundreds of metres up -- giant desert-floor drawings called geoglyphs (answer = only visible from the air / geoglyphs; teach the term; distractors at night, from the sea, by moonlight). T2: the Nazca made each line by clearing away the desert's reddish, iron-stained surface pebbles to expose the paler ground beneath, a contrast that has survived ~2,000 years because it almost never rains here (answer = the pebble-clearing method / the pale subsoil). T3 (dinner-test payoff): among more than 70 giant animal figures, the most famous is a hummingbird about 93 m across, drawn with a long thin beak and outstretched wings (answer = the hummingbird; distractors the condor, the monkey, the spider -- all real Nazca figures). T4: high on a hillside sits a robed figure with a round head and one raised hand, nicknamed 'the Astronaut' -- but archaeologists read it as an owl-headed man or shaman, not a visitor from space (answer = an owl-man / shaman figure, correcting the 'aliens' myth; distractors a god, an astronaut, a warrior). T5: the German mathematician Maria Reiche spent 40 years measuring and guarding the lines, arguing they formed a giant astronomical calendar marking solstices and star-risings -- but their true purpose stays debated, with water and fertility ritual now favoured (answer = an astronomical calendar, LABELLED as one contested theory; distractors a map, an alphabet, a calendar). Further rungs: each animal drawn as a single unbroken line that never crosses itself, hinting the figures were ceremonial walking paths; the older Paracas Candelabra etched on a coastal hillside; hundreds of faint new figures found recently by drones and AI.
source: Wikipedia: Nazca Lines (made by removing the reddish ferric-oxide pebbles to reveal paler subsoil; >70 figures incl. hummingbird ~93 m, monkey with spiral tail, spider, condor ~134 m; the 'Astronaut'/owlman; best seen from ~500 m up; Maria Reiche; purposes debated -- astronomical, water/fertility ritual, ceremonial pathways; Nazca & Paracas cultures ~500 BC-500 AD) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; credit the Nazca people's real skill -- the failure mode is von Daniken's 'runway for alien gods', which the T4 rung must correct. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the PURPOSE is genuinely DEBATED -- never assert aliens or a single settled function; Maria Reiche's calendar theory is one contested view. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 hummingbird / T4 'Astronaut' correction. LANE: the desert's aridity that preserves the lines cross-links to geography's own rain-shadow/Atacama-edge theme; no food or animal rung (the animal figures are cultural drawings, not zoology).
history_overlap: Minimal history overlap. The main hazard is the 'ancient aliens' narrative; rungs must correct it, crediting the Nazca, and flag the purpose as debated.

name: Tiwanaku and Pumapunku
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A monumental ruined city on the treeless Bolivian altiplano near Lake Titicaca, ~3,850 m up. T1: on a high plain so lofty it lies above most European mountaintops, the ruins of Tiwanaku belong to a civilization that flourished a thousand years BEFORE the Inca (answer = it predates the Inca; distractors the Maya, the Aztec, the Spanish). T2: Tiwanaku's most famous monument is a great doorway carved from a single block of stone, its lintel crowned by a central 'Staff God' figure -- the Gate of the Sun (answer = the named gateway; distractors the Gate of the Moon, the Lion Gate, the Ishtar Gate). T3 (dinner-test payoff): at the nearby temple of Pumapunku, hard andesite blocks are cut into crisp interlocking H-shapes as precise as machine-work -- craftsmanship so exact it is a magnet for 'ancient aliens' myths, though Tiwanaku's own skilled masons made them (answer = the H-shaped blocks; distractors L-shaped, T-shaped, spiral). T4: the largest single stone at Pumapunku is estimated at about 131 tonnes and was hauled to the site from a quarry up to 10 km away across the bare altiplano (answer = ~131 tonnes; number as payoff; distractors ~20 t, ~400 t, ~1,000 t). T5: to farm this frost-prone highland Tiwanaku built long raised planting beds separated by water channels that soaked up the day's heat and shielded crops from night frost -- raised-field farming called waru waru (answer = the named raised-field system; teach the term). Further rungs: the sunken temple with its wall of carved stone heads; the Akapana platform mound; the Ponce monolith; the culture's decline ~AD 1000, linked to a long drought.
source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku (elev 3,850 m, ~10 km from Lake Titicaca; largest sandstone block 7.81 m long, ~131 tonnes; precisely cut interlocking andesite/sandstone H-shaped blocks; construction ~AD 536-600, Tiwanaku peak ~AD 700-1000, predates the Inca; Gate of the Sun with Staff God/Viracocha imagery) -- verified via WebFetch. Waru waru / suka kollus raised-field farming from the Tiwanaku article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the H-blocks are the work of skilled Tiwanaku masons -- the T3 rung must credit them and rebut the 'too precise for humans/aliens' pseudo-archaeology directly. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: block weights are ESTIMATES; Tiwanaku PREDATES the Inca (a common mix-up); dates ~AD 500-1000. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 H-blocks / T5 frost-proof raised fields. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (Gate of the Sun, Pumapunku, raised fields); Tiwanaku as a polity is shared with history.
history_overlap: Tiwanaku as a civilization overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the monuments and the raised-field engineering; no rung should read as a pure political-history episode.

name: Caral
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A city of earthen pyramids in the Supe Valley on Peru's desert coast -- among the oldest cities in the Americas. T1: in a dry Peruvian river valley stand six earthen pyramids raised around 2600 BC -- at the very same time the Egyptians were building the pyramids of Giza on the far side of the world -- making Caral among the oldest cities in ALL the Americas (answer = the oldest city in the Americas; the 2600 BC / same-era-as-Giza hook constructs the superlative; distractors the largest, the highest, the driest). T2: a city of thousands left something startling OUT -- archaeologists have found no defensive walls, no weapons, and no mutilated bodies, no sign of war (answer = the absence of warfare; FLAG as 'no evidence found', not a proven utopia; distractors no farming, no religion, no trade). T3 (dinner-test payoff): instead of weapons, Caral's ruins gave up 32 flutes made from condor and pelican bone -- this was a musical, ceremonial city (answer = the bone flutes; distractors knives, coins, mirrors). T4: sunk below ground level in the heart of Caral is a round plaza where the whole community could gather for ritual, facing the great pyramid -- a sunken circular court (answer = the sunken circular plaza; distractors a ball court, a reservoir, an amphitheatre). T5: Caral had no pottery at all -- a 'preceramic' city -- yet its people knotted a length of string that may be the oldest known quipu in the Andes, the knotted record-keeping device the Inca would use 4,000 years later (answer = the quipu; teach the term). Further rung: the ~28 m Piramide Mayor and the geoglyph-marked landscape around the valley.
source: Wikipedia: Caral (inhabited ~2600-2000 BC, 'the oldest city in the Americas', Norte Chico/Caral-Supe, ~1,500 years before the Olmec; contemporary with Egypt's pyramids; 'no indications of warfare -- battlements, weapons, or mutilated bodies'; preceramic; a knotted-textile quipu found; Piramide Mayor 150 x 110 x 28 m) -- verified via WebFetch. The 32 bone flutes (condor and pelican bone) and sunken circular plazas from the Caral / Caral-Supe articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate a sophisticated early city -- but the T2 'no war' rung must be framed as ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE, not a romanticised peaceful-utopia myth (the stance guards against noble-savage over-claiming as much as against 'primitive'). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: dates ~2600 BC; 'no evidence of warfare found'; the quipu is an EARLY example. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 bone flutes. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (pyramids, sunken plaza, flutes, quipu); Norte Chico as a civilization is shared with history.
history_overlap: Caral/Norte Chico overlaps with the history bank as an early civilization. Keep rungs on the site; flag the 'no warfare' rung as absence-of-evidence rather than proven peace, and the quipu as an early example.

name: Chaco Canyon
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A remote high-desert canyon in New Mexico, hub of the Ancestral Puebloan world from ~850-1150 CE. T1: in a dry, almost treeless canyon the Ancestral Puebloans raised huge multi-storey stone-and-timber buildings called 'great houses'; the largest, Pueblo Bonito, once held about 650 rooms and rose four storeys (answer = the named great house; distractors Chetro Ketl, Casa Rinconada, Cliff Palace). T2 (dinner-test payoff): building the great houses swallowed the timber of some 200,000 pine trees -- and there are almost no trees in the canyon, so the heavy beams were carried by hand, with no wheels or draft animals, from mountains up to ~110 km away (answer = hauled overland on foot; distractors floated downriver, grown on-site, traded from Mexico). T3: dead-straight roads up to ~9 m wide run out of Chaco for tens of kilometres, cutting across mesas in perfectly straight lines instead of bending around obstacles (answer = the arrow-straight roads; distractors winding, paved, downhill-only). T4: high on Fajada Butte a spiral pecked into the rock is pierced by a 'dagger' of sunlight that splits it exactly at midday on the summer solstice -- the 'Sun Dagger' (answer = the solstice noon dagger of light; distractors midnight, the equinox sunset, the winter dawn). T5: Chaco's great houses and the great kiva of Casa Rinconada line up with the cardinal directions and with the moon's slow 18.6-year standstill cycle -- a lunar rhythm the builders tracked across generations (answer = the lunar-standstill alignment). Further rungs: the enormous circular great kivas; turquoise workshops and macaw remains showing trade reaching central Mexico; the mystery of the canyon's ~1150 depopulation.
source: Wikipedia: Chaco Culture National Historical Park (Pueblo Bonito ~650 rooms, four storeys, largest great house; ~200,000 trees hauled on foot from up to ~110 km/70 mi away; dead-straight roads up to ~9 m/30 ft wide and ~97 km/60 mi long; Fajada Butte 'Sun Dagger' spiral marking solstices/equinoxes; alignments to cardinal directions and the 18.6-year lunar standstill; ~850-1150 CE, Ancestral Puebloans) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Ancestral Puebloan astronomy and engineering as a full civilization (no 'how could they possibly...' condescension). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: prefer 'Ancestral Puebloans' over 'Anasazi'; note the Sun Dagger's alignment was documented in the 1970s and has since shifted with erosion. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T2 timber hauled 110 km by hand, or the T4 Sun Dagger. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (great houses, roads, Sun Dagger, alignments); Ancestral Puebloan history is shared.
history_overlap: Ancestral Puebloan history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the great houses, roads, timber, and the Sun Dagger, not a general culture-history ladder.

name: Mesa Verde
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: Ancestral Puebloan villages tucked into sandstone alcoves in the canyon walls of southwestern Colorado. T1: in Colorado, the Ancestral Puebloans built entire stone villages NOT on the flat mesa top but inside natural rock alcoves partway down the cliff faces -- cliff dwellings sheltered under overhangs (answer = built into the cliff faces / alcoves; distractors in caves underground, in treetops, on riverbanks). T2: the largest cliff dwelling in all of North America, with about 150 rooms and 23 round ceremonial chambers, is Cliff Palace (answer = the named dwelling; distractors Balcony House, Spruce Tree House, Long House). T3: those round sunken rooms, entered by ladder through a hole in the roof, were ceremonial chambers called kivas (answer = the named/teach term; distractors cenotes, kachinas, hogans). T4: the alcove villages face south and southwest so the low winter sun warms them while the overhang shades them in summer -- clever passive-solar design (answer = oriented to the sun for winter warmth/summer shade; distractors oriented for defence, for drainage, toward a river). T5 (dinner-test payoff): around 1300 CE the Ancestral Puebloans left Mesa Verde entirely and moved south -- and tree-rings preserved in their own roof-beams reveal the trigger: a decades-long drought in the late 1200s (answer = the drought, read from tree-rings; teach that dendrochronology dates it). Further rung: the descendants are today's Pueblo peoples -- the builders did not 'vanish'.
source: Wikipedia: Mesa Verde National Park & Cliff Palace (Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings in sandstone alcoves; Cliff Palace ~150 rooms and 23 kivas, largest cliff dwelling in North America; kivas as round sunken ceremonial rooms; depopulation ~1300 CE tied to the late-1200s 'Great Drought' via tree-ring dating; descendants are modern Pueblo peoples). Grokipedia cross-check recommended (WebSearch budget exhausted; corroborate the room/kiva counts and the drought dating at build time).
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the builders are a living people (today's Pueblo nations) -- never 'the vanished/mysterious Anasazi'. Lead with the scene of villages hidden in the cliff. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the ~1300 abandonment is dated by TREE-RINGS to the late-1200s drought (say how we know); descendants persist. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 tree-ring-dated drought. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (alcove villages, Cliff Palace, kivas, the drought); Ancestral Puebloan history is shared.
history_overlap: Ancestral Puebloan history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the alcove architecture and the drought abandonment; frame the builders as ancestors of living Pueblo peoples, not a vanished-race history episode.

name: Monte Alban
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The Zapotec capital built on a flattened mountaintop high above the Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico. T1 (dinner-test payoff): to build their capital the Zapotec did something staggering to a mountain -- they levelled its whole summit flat, some 400 m above the valley floor, to make a giant plaza in the sky (answer = they flattened/levelled the mountaintop; distractors hollowed it out, terraced the sides, tunnelled through it). T2: around that plaza stand carved stone slabs of contorted human figures, long called 'los Danzantes' (the dancers) but now read as slain or sacrificed war captives (answer = the reinterpretation as captives, not dancers; FLAG the changed interpretation; distractors dancers, ballplayers, priests). T3: one building at Monte Alban, 'Building J', is shaped like an arrowhead and set at an odd angle to everything around it, most likely to line up with a star (answer = an arrowhead shape / astronomical alignment; distractors a pyramid, a circle, a cross). T4: Building J's carved slabs, showing upside-down heads beneath place-signs, are thought to be a list of the towns the Zapotec conquered (answer = conquered towns; distractors a king-list, a star-map, a calendar). T5: the Zapotec of Monte Alban carved some of the EARLIEST writing and calendar glyphs in Mesoamerica -- dots-and-bars dates that were an early step toward written language in the Americas (answer = early writing/hieroglyphs). Further rung: the ball court and the elite tombs with painted murals.
source: Wikipedia: Monte Alban (Zapotec capital on an artificially levelled ridge ~1,940 m elevation, rising ~400 m from the valley floor; the Danzantes -- over 300 slabs, once thought dancers, now interpreted as tortured/sacrificed war prisoners; Building J arrow-shaped and rotated, astronomical significance, aligned to Capella; conquest-slab place-signs; founded ~500 BC; some of the earliest Zapotec writing/calendar) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the levelled-mountain feat and the early writing celebrate Zapotec engineering and intellect. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the Danzantes are 'once thought dancers, now read as slain captives' -- state the reinterpretation, don't pick one silently. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 flattened mountaintop. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the levelled summit, the Danzantes, Building J, early writing); Zapotec history is shared.
history_overlap: Zapotec history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the site (levelled summit, Danzantes, Building J, early glyphs); frame the conquest-slab rung as a place-artifact, not a conquest narrative.

name: Tulum
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: A walled Maya port perched on a low cliff above the turquoise Caribbean, on the Yucatan coast of Mexico. T1 (dinner-test payoff): almost every great Maya city hides inland in the jungle -- but Tulum sits right on a cliff over the sea, the only major Maya city built on the coast, above the Caribbean (answer = the Caribbean Sea / the coastal setting; distractors the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic). T2: Tulum was a walled trading town, and its Maya name was Zama, meaning 'dawn', because its cliff faces the sunrise over the sea (answer = 'dawn'/sunrise; distractors 'wall', 'harbour', 'star'). T3: Tulum guarded the coastal trade in obsidian, jade and salt, and its clifftop temple, El Castillo, is thought to have doubled as a beacon -- lined up with a gap in the offshore reef to guide trading canoes safely in (answer = a navigation beacon/lighthouse for canoes; FLAG as an interpretation; distractors a prison, a granary, a ball court).
source: Wikipedia: Tulum (walled Postclassic Maya port on the Caribbean cliff coast; ancient name Zama meaning 'dawn/sunrise'; thrived 13th-15th c. as a trade port for obsidian, jade, salt; El Castillo clifftop temple with a possible reef-gap navigational/beacon function). Grokipedia cross-check recommended (WebSearch budget exhausted; corroborate the beacon interpretation and the 'Zama' gloss at build time).
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; Tulum's magic is the setting -- a Maya city on a Caribbean beach. Lead with the cliff-over-turquoise-sea scene. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the El Castillo reef-beacon function is an INTERPRETATION -- flag it, don't assert it. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 clifftop Caribbean setting. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the coastal siting, the name, the beacon); Maya trade history is shared.
history_overlap: Maya coastal-trade history overlaps lightly with the history bank. Keep the mini on the place (its clifftop setting, its name, its beacon), not a trade-network history ladder.

name: Chan Chan
strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
scope: The Chimu capital sprawling near Trujillo on Peru's north desert coast. T1 (dinner-test payoff): near the Peruvian coast lies the largest city ever built of mud brick in the Americas -- 20 square kilometres of walls made not of stone but of adobe, sun-dried earth (answer = mud brick / adobe; distractors stone, coral, timber). T2: Chan Chan's tall adobe walls are carved with endless friezes of fish and waves and seabirds -- fitting art for the Chimu, a people of the ocean and its fisheries (answer = fish and sea creatures; distractors jaguars, condors, maize). T3: this desert megacity of tens of thousands was conquered around 1470 by the Inca, who absorbed the Chimu into their empire (answer = the Inca; distractors the Aztec, the Spanish, the Wari).
source: Wikipedia: Chan Chan (Chimor/Chimu capital near Trujillo; 'the largest city of the pre-Columbian era in South America' and the largest adobe city in the Americas; ~20 sq km; nine-to-ten walled royal ciudadelas; adobe friezes of fish, waves, nets, and seabirds; built from ~850 CE, conquered by the Inca ~1470; peak population ~40,000-60,000) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the marvel is scale in an unexpected material -- the largest earthen city on Earth. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: 'largest ADOBE/mud-brick city in the Americas' (largest pre-Columbian city in South America) -- keep the superlative precise. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 mud-brick megacity. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the adobe scale, the sea friezes); Chimu/Inca political history is shared. Note: the sea-friezes rung is about the CARVED PLACE, not fish biology (that would be the animal bank).
history_overlap: Chimu and Inca history overlap with the history bank. Keep the mini on the place (adobe scale, wall friezes); the conquest rung names the later empire as a place-fact, not a conquest narrative.
